kalodvalitametacca cittattvaṃ kartṛtāmayam | acidrūpasya śūnyāderbhitaṃ guṇatayā sthitam || (3 | 22) iti vakṣyate | prathāṃ nīyate iti | atrāpi vakṣyamāṇanayena iti saṃbandhaḥ | vakṣyate hi mukhyatvaṃ kartṛtāyāstu bodhasya ca cidātmanaḥ | śūnyādau tadguṇe jñānaṃ tatsamāveśalakṣaṇam || 3 | 23) iti | tacca idaṃ cidrūpasya anyatra anupakaraṇīkaraṇaṃ śarīrādau, kāyaprāṇādervā kāyādirūpatānimajjanena cidrūpatodrecanamiti | etadeva prabhāvaḥ-prakarṣeṇa yadvaśāt bhāvyate anyavilakṣaṇatayā ca kartavyaṃ bhāvayatīti | etacca parāparasiddhiprādhānyeneti (page 87) vakṣyāmaḥ | siddhasya iti svarūpato jñaptitaśca | nanu ca siddhe vastuni yat pramāṇaṃ, tat kila vyavahārasādhanamiti prasiddham | tataśca tadanusāreṇaiva vṛttau vācyaṃ pratyabhijñānamātraṃ sādhyate itītyāśaṅkya āha sarva iti | jaḍapadārthaviṣaye hi siddhe'pi yat pramāṇaṃ vyavahārasādhanaṃ, tadavaśyamasiddhasya kasyacidaṃśasya antatastathā prakhyopākhyārūpasya vyavahārasaṃpattimapūrvāṃ karoti | ātmani tu īśvare na kiṃcidasaṃpannaṃ sādhyamasti prakhyopākhyayorapi siddhatvāt, tadasiddhau prameyaleśasyāpi hi na kācit siddhiriti uktam | atastadvyavahāramātramapi neha sādhyate, apitu upāṃśu cchannaṃ sthitaṃ sat, upasamīpe iti hṛdayasaṃgamanena pradhānatayā darśyate | ātmani īśvararūpe ye prakhyopākhye te mā anyatra dehādau nīlādau ca upakaraṇīye bhavetām, apitu te eva pradhānatayā paśyateti | tena vṛttau sūtrānusāreṇaiva upadarśyate iti uktam | loke jaḍaviṣaye yat vyavahāramātrasya sādhanaṃ, tadapi iha ajaḍe kriyamāṇaṃ pradarśanena samamavikalaṃ pradarśanamātrāvaśeṣaṃ pradarśanena ca paśya-paśyeti avadhānadāpanārūpeṇa tulyam | tadatra sūtre dṛṣṭe iti karmaṇi dṛṣṭāntā- veśena akarmakatvāt kartari eva dārṣṭāntikābhiprāyeṇa vyākhyāne nirvivādasiddhatā nāma dṛṣṭatvamubhayatra tulyam || 3 || bhāvisūtrārthaṃ saṃkṣepeṇa nirūpayati evaṃ ca iti | ātmaiva īśvaraḥ, sa ca siddhaḥ iti yaduktam, tadevaṃ; tasya yā pratyabhijñā karaṇabhāvasādhana- tvena āviṣkriyamāṇā śaktistatkṛtaśca dṛḍhaniścayaḥ, tadapi eva
**The self is the Lord: what the recognition does** The kārikā declares that the self alone is the Lord. And at once a sharp objection arises. A valid means of knowledge, it is said, establishes what was *not* established before — it serves the practical dealings of the world. But the Lord-self, on our own showing, is already established. So what could a pramāṇa possibly do here? What is there left for it to prove? Abhinavagupta's answer turns this objection around. For an inert object, even an established one, the pramāṇa does indeed make a new attainment — it brings out some part that was not yet grasped, at least the manifestation and the designation (prakhyā and upākhyā) of the thing in our dealing with it. But in the self — the Lord — there is nothing un-attained to be established. The manifestation and the designation are already there; without them, not even a trace of a thing could be known at all. So the pramāṇa here is not establishing something new. What, then, is it doing? It is *foregrounding* what is already present but hidden. The recognition (pratyabhijñā) does not bring the Lord into being; it brings the Lord, who was always near and always present, into the *foreground of our own awareness*. As Abhinavagupta says, what is hidden and standing close by is shown as primary, by the coming-together of the heart. The recognition makes the manifestation and the designation of the self-as-Lord no longer an instrument lost among the things of the body and the world, but the primary thing that we see. It is the turning of the attention — the "see, see" — upon what was always before us. And this recognition is the very content of the whole teaching. After the upoddhāta, the opening, the whole śāstra that is to come has, as its to-be-said content, the recognition — which is the jñāna-kriyā, the knowledge-and-action power, made firm by the conviction (dṛḍhaniścaya) that arises from it. The two powers — knowledge and action — are determined at length throughout the work, and the firm conviction in the self-as-Lord is their fruit. So the point is this: the self is the Lord, and he is already established — not to be newly proved, but to be *recognized*. The pramāṇa does not reach out to a distant, un-known thing; it turns the light of attention upon the one who was always the knower and the known, the one standing near in the very act of knowing. The recognition is not the acquisition of something new; it is the foregrounding of the self, the Lord, who was never absent. And this, the firm conviction in the self-as-Lord, is what the whole teaching sets before us. ---

> The question is what a valid means does here at all. A pramāṇa is supposed to establish what is not > yet established; but the self is already the Lord, so a pramāṇa for it seems idle. Abhinavagupta's > reply is that the pramāṇa does not establish a new thing — it foregrounds what is already present but > hidden. Recognition does not bring the Lord into being; it brings the Lord, who was always present, > into the foreground of awareness. The self moves from the background — an instrument lost among the > things of the body and the world — to the primary thing seen. Nothing in the content changes; what > changes is where the self stands. > > The passage does not by itself establish that the self is ontologically the Lord; that claim is > argued elsewhere. Its point here is narrower: it gives recognition a mechanism (foregrounding), so > that the recognition-thesis does not collapse into either adding a new fact or doing nothing.
